\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{しあわせ} (shiawase)}{しあわせ (shiawase)}]{\ja{しあわせ} (shiawase) — happy}

\label{lesson:JA-C126-shiawase}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for very young, then the Japanese for plentiful.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{しあわせ}}
\textbf{\ja{しあわせ}} — \emph{shiawase} — \textquotedblleft{}happy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{しあわせ}} (\emph{shiawase}) is native. JMdict's older spelling shows \emph{shi}, from \emph{suru}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{awase}, \textquotedblleft{}fitting together\textquotedblright{}; it is usually explained as first meaning how things fell out, good or bad. It is inherited rather than borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{あんしん} (anshin)}{あんしん (anshin)}]{\ja{あんしん} (anshin) — relieved}

\label{lesson:JA-C126-anshin}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for happy, then the Japanese for drowsy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{あんしん}}
\textbf{\ja{あんしん}} — \emph{anshin} — \textquotedblleft{}relieved\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{あんしん}} (\emph{anshin}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{an}, \textquotedblleft{}peaceful\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{'an}) and \emph{shin}, \textquotedblleft{}heart, mind\textquotedblright{} (\emph{sim}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese after Baxter–Sagart).
\end{cousinweb}
